The 1.5x target was not reached and is out of reach by restructuring: the reference headroom is 0.97 to 1.0, so the baseline already streams A (268 MB read + 268 MB written) at the memory floor, and A must be read once and written once (the 'touch each element once' case; only x is re-read per row, from cache, and sharing it measured nothing). The winning state replaces rocBLAS's one-workgroup-per-row, 1024-thread, strided per-thread loop with loop-free one-wave workgroups (block 64, grid (cdiv(M,256), N)), each thread doing one global_load_dwordx4 of x and of A, two v_pk_fma and one x4 store (16 B per lane, 1 KB contiguous per wave), with a scalar tail path for M not a multiple of 4.

friction: list_states shows action 'coarsen' for earlier states without the factor: I could not tell which factors had already been tried on ref without opening each state.

The memory floor model put the winning state at headroom 0.90 (5.7 TB/s combined) and ref at 0.97-1.06 across runs: the floor (20 us + read/4.5 + written/10.7) is about 10 % pessimistic for a read-modify-write of the same array, so 'headroom 1.0' understated what was available (1.11x was found). A floor fitted for in-place update kernels would be a better guide.

reference_headroom moved between 0.97 and 1.06 between bench calls of different candidates (reference_ms 0.101 to 0.1105): a single stable reference figure per session would make it easier to rank candidates benched in separate calls.

No way to express non-temporal / streaming stores or to avoid the read of x per row other than restructuring; nothing at the machine level was left to do on a 6-instruction straight-line body (2 loads, 1 wait, 2 pk_fma, 1 store).
lessons: rb_ger (in-place rank-1 update, 268 MB read + 268 MB written, baseline 0.1045 ms at headroom ~1.0): loop-free one-wave workgroups with 16 B per lane (block 64, 1 KB contiguous per wave) gave 1.108x (240 pairs). This is the same lever and the same size of gain as fi_silu_and_mul (1.03-1.06x), slightly larger here.
Block size at 16 B per lane, loop-free: block 64 1.11x, block 128 1.09x, block 256 1.076x, block 1024 0.97x. One wave per workgroup reading 1 KB contiguous is best; 4 KB per workgroup loses.
Bytes per lane at block 64: 8 B 0.78x, 16 B 1.11x, 32 B 0.956x. At block 1024, 4 B per lane loop-free is 0.70x. 16 B per lane (one dwordx4) is a sharp optimum.

Sharing the cached, re-read vector x between rows does not pay: 2 rows per workgroup 1.108x (equal to 1 row), 4 rows 1.075x. The re-read of x per row (as many bytes as A, but from cache) is free next to the cold A stream.
coarsen factor 2 on the loop-free block-64 state: 1.104x against 1.108x for the parent, no gain. Order of the two loads (cold A first vs cached x first): parity (0.997).
A kernel at reference headroom 0.97-1.0 still had 11 % in it through launch geometry alone; 1.5x was not reachable (A must be read and written once).

session.final:
The 1.5x target was not reached: the best verified state is `17818752b3532917` at **1.108x** over amdclang (240 pairs, CI 1.106–1.110; 0.0942 ms against 0.1045 ms), with the full battery passing 77/77.

**Why 1.5x is out of reach:** the reference headroom is 0.97–1.0, so amdclang's build already streams `A` at the memory floor. `A` (268 MB) must be read once and written once, so this is the "each element touched once" case. Only `x` is re-read per row, and it comes from cache; loading it once for several rows gained nothing.

**What the winning state does:** it replaces rocBLAS's one workgroup per row (1024 threads, each looping over the row) with loop-free one-wave workgroups. The launch is block 64 on a grid of (cdiv(M, 256), N), and each thread handles 4 consecutive elements (16 bytes) with one wide load of `x`, one of `A`, and one wide store. A scalar tail path covers `M` not a multiple of 4.

| Variant | Speedup vs amdclang |
|---|---|
| 16 B per thread, block 64 | 1.108 (win, shipped) |
| 16 B per thread, block 128 | 1.09 (win) |
| 16 B per thread, block 256 | 1.076 (win) |
| 16 B per thread, block 1024 | 0.97 (loss) |
| 8 B per thread, block 64 | 0.78 (loss) |
| 32 B per thread, block 64 | 0.956 (loss) |
| 4 B per thread, block 1024 | 0.70 (loss) |
| `x` shared by 2 rows, block 64 | 1.108 (win, no gain over one row) |
| `x` shared by 4 rows, block 64 | 1.075 (win, below one row) |
| `coarsen` factor 2 on the best state | 1.104 (win, no gain) |

Issuing the `A` load before the `x` load measured parity against the best state (0.997), so I stopped after three different kinds of idea brought under 1 % each.

The report is recorded with the full list of what was tried, the friction and the lessons. The main friction item is that the memory-floor model is about 10 % pessimistic for an in-place update like this one, so a headroom of 1.0 understated what was available.
